title: I/O models: blocking, epoll and io_uring
goal: By the end, you can explain what a program's thread does while it waits for data on a connection, how one thread can wait on thousands of connections with epoll, what Java does underneath when it waits, and why io_uring works differently and is often switched off.
opening:
Picture a quiet Sunday morning at the small company whose program records card payments for coffee shops. Card readers in 2,000 shops stay connected to the program all day, ready to send a payment the moment someone taps a card. At 7 a.m. hardly anyone is buying coffee. The program has almost nothing to do, yet it holds about 200 MB of memory.

It's easy to think that waiting is free. A waiting program uses no CPU, and in a test with ten card readers nothing looks wrong. The cost hides in how it waits.

File systems: inodes, links and file descriptors showed that every network connection is a file descriptor, like an open file. In this lesson, we'll watch a read on one fall asleep, teach one thread (one line of work inside a program) to wait on thousands of connections with a Linux call named epoll, see how Java does this for you, and meet io_uring, which hands the kernel the work itself. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments program keeps 2,000 network connections open, one to each card reader, and most of them are quiet. It's written the simple way, with one thread per connection, where a thread is one line of work that the operating system runs. How many threads does the operating system see, and what are they doing?
options: About 12, one per CPU core, taking turns over the connections
About 2,000, almost all asleep in `read()`, using no CPU
About 2,000, each running at full speed to check its connection
One: the kernel shares a single thread between all the connections
warmup.why: In the lab box, a program like that had 2,028 threads, and `ps` showed 2,000 of them asleep in the kernel, waiting for data on their connections. Sleeping threads use no CPU, which rules out the third option. But each one is a task the kernel tracks, with memory set aside for it: the program held about 190 to 230 MB. The last option describes what epoll and Java's `Selector` let a program do, and the program has to be written for it. The first section shows a sleeping thread up close.

sections.h: Waiting for one connection: a blocking read goes to sleep
sections.body:
`wait.c` is a small C program that waits for a reply on a connection. A child process, a copy of the program made with the system call `fork`, plays the bank and answers one second later. The parent's `read()` returns after 1.00 s, and in that second it used 0.00 s of CPU time, the time it spent running on the processor (the CPU). While it waited, `ps`, a command that lists processes, showed it in state `S` (asleep), inside a kernel function called `unix_stream_read_generic`. So a waiting program sleeps. Who wakes it?

`wait.c` talks through a socket, one end of a connection. Like an open file, a socket gets a file descriptor (fd), the small number a program passes in every call about it. Bytes from the network don't go straight into your program. The kernel, the core of the operating system, keeps a **receive queue** for every socket, and its network code adds arriving bytes to it whether anyone is reading or not. `read()` copies from that queue. If the queue is empty, the kernel puts the calling thread to sleep on the socket's wait queue, a list of who's waiting for it, and runs something else. (CPU scheduling: EEVDF, nice and CPU quotas showed how the kernel picks what runs next.) When a packet, a small parcel of bytes from the network, arrives, the kernel adds its bytes to the queue and wakes the threads waiting on that socket.

That's a **blocking read**, and it's the simplest way to wait there is. A program that asks a database for some rows usually waits for the answer exactly like this.

The queue has a size. In the lab box, a TCP socket's receive queue starts at 128 KB. (TCP is the set of rules that carries a stream of bytes reliably between two computers.) The setting `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` reads `4096 131072 6291456`, the minimum, the default and the maximum, and the kernel grows the queue for fast senders. When nobody reads and it fills up, TCP tells the sender to stop, so a slow reader slows the writer down instead of losing data. A server, a program that waits for others to connect to it, waits in one more place. Its listening socket keeps a queue of new connections, and `accept()` sleeps on it until a client connects.

A restaurant can work this way. Give every table its own waiter, who stands by it until the guests decide. In program terms, the waiter is the thread, the table is the connection, and standing there is the blocking read. It's easy to run, and the bill grows with the number of tables, busy or not.

The limit is that a thread waiting on one socket can't wait on anything else. A server that wants 2,000 clients at once, most of them quiet, needs 2,000 threads: one thread per connection. `EchoServers`, a small Java server that sends back whatever it receives, works this way in `threads` mode. With 2,000 idle clients connected, it had 2,028 threads, and 2,000 of them were asleep in the kernel function `wait_woken`. Its RSS (resident set size), the memory it really used, was about 190 to 230 MB.

Each of those threads is a task the kernel tracks (Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS). Each reserves a stack, its own scratch memory for the functions it's running. That's about 2 MB set aside on the lab box's arm64 Linux, though only the parts a thread touches take real memory. (arm64 is the chip family in recent Macs.) Each counts against `pids.max`, the cap on tasks in a container, the boxed-off Linux system that Docker runs. And each wake-up is a context switch, where the CPU stops one task and starts another, which costs time. At 10,000 connections the numbers get uncomfortable. The problem got its name in 1999: C10K, ten thousand clients on one server.

What we want instead is one thread that waits on many sockets at once and is told which ones have data. Getting there takes two steps: a read that refuses to wait, and a call that waits on a whole set.

try.title: Watch a read sleep
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab box: `docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box`.
Read `os/c/l11/wait.c`. A child process plays the bank and writes `APPROVED` one second after the start, and the parent waits for it. Mode `block` is a plain `read()`.
Predict the state that `ps` shows half a second in, and how long `strace -T` says the `read` took. (`strace` prints every system call a program makes, and `-T` adds the time spent in each.)

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
gcc -O2 -o /tmp/wait os/c/l11/wait.c
/tmp/wait block & sleep 0.5; ps -o pid,stat,wchan:22,comm -C wait; wait
strace -T -e trace=read /tmp/wait block 2>&1 | grep -E '^read|^block'

try.expect:
PIDs differ:

```text
  PID STAT WCHAN                  COMMAND
   12 S    unix_stream_read_gener wait
   14 S    hrtimer_nanosleep      wait
block got 8 bytes after 1.00 s; read() failed with EAGAIN 0 times; CPU used 0.00 s
read(3, "\177ELF\2\1\1\3\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\0\3\0\267\0\1\0\0\0\360\206\2\0\0\0\0\0"..., 832) = 832 <0.000469>
read(3, "APPROVED", 64)                 = 8 <1.004026>
block got 8 bytes after 1.00 s; read() failed with EAGAIN 0 times; CPU used 0.00 s
```

Both processes are asleep (`S`). The parent waits in `unix_stream_read_generic`, the kernel's read for this kind of socket, and the child sleeps in a timer. `strace -T` prints the time spent inside each call. The read at start-up, of the C library (the shared code every C program loads), took half a millisecond. The read of the reply took 1.004 s, all of it asleep. The CPU time stays at 0.00 s.

sections.h: Waiting for many connections: non-blocking reads and epoll
sections.body:
`wait.c spin` waits for the same reply another way. It makes the socket non-blocking and calls `read()` in a loop. In one second, its reads failed 1,335,566 times, and it burned a full second of CPU, for the same 8 bytes the blocking version got for free.

A socket opened with the flag `O_NONBLOCK` never puts a thread to sleep. `read()` returns data if the queue has some, and otherwise fails at once with the error `EAGAIN` ("try again"). Now one thread could serve 2,000 sockets by trying each in turn. But most tries fail, and the loop spins at 100% CPU even when every client is quiet. In the restaurant, that's one waiter who runs from table to table all evening, asking "Ready yet?" The missing piece is a call that sleeps until any socket in a set has data.

The first answer was `select()`, from BSD, a version of Unix built at the University of California, Berkeley, in the early 1980s. You pass a bitmap of descriptors, one bit per fd number. The kernel checks each one, sleeps if none is ready, and hands back the bitmap of the ready ones. It caps fd numbers at 1,024 (`FD_SETSIZE`), and every call copies the whole set into the kernel and checks every socket in it. `poll()` drops the cap but keeps the cost: each call takes time in proportion to the number of connections, not the number that have data. With 2,000 connections and 3 active, every wake-up checks 2,000.

Linux 2.6 added **epoll**, which separates signing up from waiting. `epoll_create1` makes an epoll instance, a waiting list that lives in the kernel. `epoll_ctl(ADD)` registers a socket once, in the instance's **interest list**. From then on, data arriving on that socket puts it on the instance's **ready list**. `epoll_wait` sleeps until that list has something on it and returns only what's there, so idle sockets cost nothing per call. On arm64 the system call is named `epoll_pwait`, in the same way that `open` is really `openat`. BSD and macOS have the same idea under the name `kqueue`.

In the restaurant, epoll is a bell on every table. The waiter registers each bell once, sits down, and walks only to the tables that rang. A thread that lives in this wait-and-handle cycle is called an **event loop**.

epoll can report a socket in two ways, and the difference bites. **Level-triggered**, the default, reports a socket for as long as it has data to read. Read half of it, and the next `epoll_wait` returns the socket again: the bell keeps ringing until the table has ordered everything. **Edge-triggered** (`EPOLLET`) reports it once each time new data arrives. Read half and wait, and the other half sits in the queue until the client sends more. It won't, if it's waiting for your answer. The bell rang once, and the waiter only took half the order. Edge-triggered code gets fewer wake-ups, which some servers want, and pays for them with code that must never stop reading early.

**With edge-triggered epoll, a read that stops early strands data. Read until `EAGAIN`.**

Here the restaurant picture breaks. A bell costs the restaurant nothing, while every socket in an interest list costs the kernel a little memory. And waiters are expensive, while threads are cheap until there are thousands of them. The stepper shows both servers and both modes. Next, we'll find this same loop inside Java.

sections.h: How Java waits: the Selector and virtual threads use epoll
sections.body:
Here's the same echo server written three ways, with the same 2,000 mostly quiet clients connected, in the lab box. "OS threads" counts the threads the kernel sees. A platform thread is Java's name for an ordinary thread that the kernel runs; virtual threads come later in this section.

| server | OS threads | RSS | system calls per echo |
|---|---|---|---|
| platform thread per connection | 2,028 | 189 to 228 MB | `read`, `write` |
| one thread with a `Selector` | 19 | 51 MB | `epoll_pwait`, `read`, `write` |
| virtual thread per connection | 33 | 67 to 75 MB | `read` (fails), `epoll_ctl`, `epoll_pwait`, `read`, `write` |

Look at the middle row first. It's written with Java NIO (new input/output), Java's library for non-blocking network code. On Linux, `Selector.open()` is `epoll_create1`, `channel.register(selector, OP_READ)` is `epoll_ctl(ADD)`, and `selector.select()` is `epoll_wait`. (On macOS the JDK, the kit that builds and runs Java programs, uses `kqueue` instead.) The loop selects, walks the list of ready connections, accepts or reads each one, and selects again. `strace -c`, which counts system calls, shows one `epoll_pwait`, one `read` and one `write` per echo, and the quiet connections cost nothing. Netty, a popular Java library for building network servers, is built on this loop, and so are the network parts of many programs later in this course.

The price is in how you write code. Nothing in the loop may block, because one blocked handler stops all 2,000 connections. It's the one waiter who stops to chat at a table while every other bell goes unanswered. So work that waits, such as asking a bank to approve a payment, has to be cut into pieces. You send the request, go back to the loop, and finish the work in a callback, a function that runs when the answer arrives.

The third row is the first server's code, unchanged, started on virtual threads. A virtual thread is a thread that the JVM, the Java virtual machine that runs Java code, manages itself. Many of them take turns on a few real threads, called carriers, as Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS showed. Its `read()` looks blocking, but the JDK made every socket non-blocking underneath. When a read finds nothing, the JDK registers the socket with epoll and parks the virtual thread: it sets it aside and frees its carrier for other work. One real thread, `MasterPoller`, sleeps in `epoll_wait` for all of them. When a socket becomes ready, it makes that virtual thread runnable again, and the read is repeated. `strace` shows the pattern: 596 reads, half of them failing with `EAGAIN`, and 585 `epoll_ctl` calls. The kernel sees 12 carriers, the poller and the JVM's own threads.

So with virtual threads, you write plain blocking code and the JDK runs an event loop for you. That's why they suit programs that spend most of their time waiting on connections. RSS lands between the other two rows. A parked virtual thread keeps its stack frames, the notes on what each function was doing, on the heap, the JVM's memory for objects. That's small, but not free.

**Never block inside an event loop. Write non-blocking code for the loop, or blocking code on virtual threads.**

epoll works well for sockets, which can say when they have data. Files are another matter, and the last section shows why.

aside.title: If virtual threads do this for me, why does anyone still write event loops?
aside.body: Virtual threads became a full part of Java in JDK 21, in 2023, and event loops are decades older, so a lot of working code and many libraries, Netty among them, are built on loops. A hand-written loop also gives full control over every byte and every wake-up, which matters for servers with huge numbers of connections. Virtual threads have costs of their own: a parked one still keeps its stack on the heap, and some kinds of waiting, such as a call into code written in C, hold on to a carrier. For a program that mostly waits, plain blocking code on virtual threads is usually the simpler choice.

sections.h: io_uring: handing the kernel the work, and why it's often blocked
sections.body:
`fio` is a tool that measures disks. Here it reads random 4 KB blocks from a file, from one thread. It skips the page cache, the kernel's copy of file data in memory (The page cache, writeback and fsync), so every read goes to the disk. With plain `pread`, a read at a given place in the file, one at a time, it managed 300 to 1,800 reads a second in the shared virtual machine. With io_uring and 32 reads waiting at once, it managed 15,900 to 23,200.

epoll answers one question: which sockets can I read without waiting? For a regular file, it has no answer. A file always counts as ready, so `epoll_ctl` refuses to watch one, with the error `EPERM`. A `read()` of a part of a file that isn't in the page cache waits in the kernel until the disk answers, whatever epoll says. So for files, the only way to have 32 reads waiting on the disk at once was 32 threads. And with epoll, every read is still a system call of its own, after the call that said it was ready.

**io_uring**, added in Linux 5.1 (2019), asks a different question. The program and the kernel share two ring buffers in memory, queues whose end wraps round to their start. The program writes requests into the **submission queue**: read this file descriptor, at this offset, into this buffer. The kernel carries them out, for files or sockets, and writes a result for each into the **completion queue**. One `io_uring_enter` call can submit many requests and wait for many results. In its polling modes, a busy program needs no system call at all. In one `fio` run under `strace`, 116,000 reads took 8,944 `io_uring_enter` calls.

Back in the restaurant, io_uring is ordering by slip. The waiter drops a stack of order slips at the kitchen window, and later picks up a tray of finished dishes. Nobody asks the kitchen "can I order now?" before every dish. That's the difference between the two models. epoll is a readiness model: it tells you when you can act. io_uring is a completion model: it tells you the work is done.

io_uring is also a large, young part of the kernel that does a lot of work for a program, and it has had many security bugs. Google reported in June 2023 that 60% of the Linux kernel exploits (programs that use a bug to break in) sent to its bug-reward program used io_uring. It had paid about 1 million US dollars for io_uring bugs alone. It had switched io_uring off on its own servers and on ChromeOS, and blocked it for Android apps. Docker 25 added the three io_uring system calls to its default seccomp filter, the list of system calls a container may not make. (What a kernel does: system calls and user mode met it.) So in the lab box, `io_uring_setup` fails with `EPERM`. The kernel has its own switch, `kernel.io_uring_disabled`: 0 allows everyone, 1 allows only privileged processes (ones with the administrator's rights) and members of `kernel.io_uring_group`, and 2 allows nobody.

For Java programs this is mostly a note to keep. Java's NIO and virtual threads use epoll on Linux. Netty offers io_uring as an alternative to epoll, and before you choose it, check that the containers your program will run in allow it.

**io_uring is fast and often blocked. Check that it's allowed before you build on it.**

The lab builds epoll's ready list as a small model, then a real `Selector` server on top.

lab.title: Build epoll's ready list, then a real Selector echo server
steps: Read `Readiness.kt`. It's a small model of the kernel's side: `Kernel` delivers bytes with `arrive`, answers a read of an empty socket with EAGAIN, and tells every `Epoll` about arrivals through `onArrive`. `Poll` is written for you, to compare.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All twelve fail.

Write `Epoll.wait`: walk the ready list oldest first, and count each entry you look at in `examined`. LEVEL reports a socket that still has data and keeps it on the list (and drops it quietly once it hasn't); EDGE reports it and removes it.

Write `EventLoop.turn`: one `wait`, then read `chunk` bytes from each ready socket, once, or, with `drain`, until the kernel says `Again`. Record data in `received`. On `Eof` the client has closed: add the socket to `closed` and remove it from the epoll.

Write `NioEchoServer.loop` in `NioEcho.kt`, following the comment above it. The tests connect 200 real clients over localhost, the computer's own network address, and check that one thread served them all.
hints: In `wait`, use the ready set's `iterator()` and `it.remove()`, so you can drop entries while you walk them.
`do { ... } while (drain && more)` reads at least once, and keeps going only in drain mode while the last read returned data.
In the NIO loop, call `keys.remove()` for every selected key. The `Selector` never clears its selected set itself, so a key you leave there is handled again on the next turn.
A read of -1 means the client closed: cancel the key, close the channel and lower `connections`, or the third test waits forever for 0.

drill.title: A Selector loop from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the Kotlin for an echo server on port 9000 that runs on one thread with a `Selector`. Set it up, accept clients, read and send back what they send, and handle a client that closes. Then say which line becomes which system call on Linux.

recap: A blocking `read()` sleeps until data reaches the socket's receive queue. It uses no CPU, but it ties up a thread: 2,000 connections meant 2,028 threads and about 200 MB.
`O_NONBLOCK` makes `read()` fail with `EAGAIN` instead of sleeping. A loop of failing reads burns a whole CPU, so something must say which sockets are ready.

`select` and `poll` check every connection on every call. epoll registers sockets once (`epoll_ctl`) and keeps a ready list that `epoll_wait` returns, so quiet connections cost nothing. Level-triggered reports a socket while it has data; edge-triggered reports it once per arrival, so that code must read until `EAGAIN`.

Java's `Selector` is epoll on Linux (kqueue on macOS), and an event loop built on it must never block. Virtual threads use it underneath: a failed read, `epoll_ctl`, a parked virtual thread, and the `MasterPoller` thread in `epoll_wait`.
io_uring is a completion model: the program and the kernel share a submission queue and a completion queue, with many operations per system call, files included.

The limit: epoll can't wait on files, and io_uring, which can, is often switched off. Docker's default seccomp filter blocks it, Google disables it in production, and `kernel.io_uring_disabled` can turn it off.
closing:
We started with a quiet Sunday morning and a program holding 200 MB of memory for 2,000 card readers that had nothing to say. Each connection had its own sleeping thread. epoll lets one thread wait for all of them, and virtual threads give you that without changing your code.

On a Linux computer you can reach, pick a running program and see where its threads sleep: `ps -L -o stat,wchan:22 -p <pid> | sort | uniq -c`. Thousands in a read means a thread per connection; a few in `do_epoll_wait` means an event loop.

Next, we'll open up the lab box itself, a container, and find an ordinary process inside. How can one kernel make a program believe it has a computer to itself?

quiz.q: From Threads, and how the JVM maps them to the OS. A Java program on JDK 25, on a computer with 8 CPU cores, handles 5,000 payments at once on virtual threads. Each one is waiting to read the bank's answer over the network. About how many operating-system threads serve those reads, and what are they doing?
options: 5,000, each asleep in `read()`
About 8 carriers that are mostly idle, plus a poller thread asleep in `epoll_wait`; the 5,000 virtual threads are parked on the heap
One, spinning on non-blocking reads
About 8 carriers, each blocked in `read()` on one connection at a time
quiz.why: A virtual thread's blocking read is a non-blocking read underneath. When it fails with `EAGAIN`, the JDK registers the socket with epoll and parks the virtual thread, which frees its carrier. One poller thread waits in `epoll_wait` for all the sockets, and makes a virtual thread runnable again when its socket is ready. The last option is the tempting one, but carriers never block in `read()` on a socket: that's the whole point. The first option describes platform threads.

quiz.q: A hand-written edge-triggered epoll loop reads 4 KB from each socket it gets an event for. A client sends a 10 KB request in one go, then waits for the answer. What happens?
options: The loop gets three events and reads all 10 KB
The kernel splits the request into 4 KB pieces, one event each
The loop reads 4 KB, and the other 6 KB wait in the receive queue with no further event; the client waits forever
`epoll_wait` returns an error because the buffer was too small
quiz.why: Edge-triggered epoll reports a socket once each time new data arrives, and the 10 KB may arrive together. After one 4 KB read, nothing new arrives, because the client is waiting for an answer, so there's no next event. Edge-triggered code must read until `EAGAIN`. The first option is close to what level-triggered epoll would do: it reports the socket again while data is left, which is why it's the forgiving default.

quiz.q: A server holds 10,000 connections, and in a typical millisecond 5 of them have data. Which statement about the cost of one wake-up is right?
options: `poll` and `epoll_wait` both check all 10,000 sockets
`poll` checks all 10,000 descriptors it was passed; `epoll_wait` returns the 5 on its ready list
`select` is fastest, because its bitmap is small
`epoll_wait` checks all 10,000, but in the kernel, so it's free
quiz.why: `poll` and `select` take the whole set on every call, and the kernel checks each descriptor, so the cost follows the number of connections. epoll registers sockets once, and the kernel adds a socket to the ready list when data arrives, so `epoll_wait` only looks at what's ready. The fourth option is tempting, but work inside the kernel still takes time. And `select` can't even handle fd numbers above 1,023.

quiz.q: A Java program that uses io_uring through Netty, a network library, starts fine on a developer's Linux laptop. Inside a Docker container, it fails at start-up with "Operation not permitted". What's the most likely cause?
options: The container's kernel is too old for io_uring
Docker's default seccomp filter blocks `io_uring_setup`, so it fails with `EPERM`
io_uring needs more memory than the container's limit
Netty can't use io_uring inside a JVM
quiz.why: Containers share the host's kernel, and the lab box's `io_uring_disabled` is 0, so the kernel allows io_uring. Docker 25 and later block the three io_uring system calls in their default seccomp filter, and the call fails with `EPERM`, which reads as "Operation not permitted". The first option is the tempting guess, but io_uring has been in Linux since 5.1 (2019), and a missing feature fails with a different error. Fall back to epoll, or run with a seccomp profile that allows io_uring if you accept the risk.

quiz.q: A program that runs once a night reads thousands of large files. A teammate wants to put the files in an epoll set, so that one thread can read them all without waiting. Why won't that work?
options: epoll only works for TCP sockets, not for other kinds of socket
epoll has a limit of 1,024 descriptors
Regular files always count as ready: `epoll_ctl` refuses them with `EPERM`, and a read of a part that isn't cached still waits for the disk
Files must be opened with `O_APPEND` to be watched
quiz.why: epoll answers "can I read without waiting?", and for a regular file the kernel has no such idea: the read waits for the disk inside the kernel. The 1,024 limit belongs to `select`, not epoll, and epoll works for every kind of socket. To wait on many file reads at once, you need several threads, or a completion API such as io_uring.

flashcards.front: What does `read()` on an empty non-blocking socket do?
flashcards.back: It fails at once with the error `EAGAIN` ("try again") instead of sleeping.

flashcards.front: What does epoll keep that `poll` doesn't?
flashcards.back: An interest list, registered once with `epoll_ctl`, and a ready list the kernel fills as data arrives. `epoll_wait` returns only the ready sockets.

flashcards.front: Level-triggered or edge-triggered: which one strands data if you read only part of it?
flashcards.back: Edge-triggered: it reports a socket once per arrival. On every event, read until `EAGAIN`.

flashcards.front: Which system calls is Java's `Selector` made of on Linux?
flashcards.back: `epoll_create1` to open it, `epoll_ctl` to register a channel, and `epoll_wait` (`epoll_pwait` on arm64) to select. On macOS it uses kqueue.

flashcards.front: What happens when a virtual thread's read on a connection finds no data?
flashcards.back: The JDK registers the socket with epoll and parks the virtual thread, freeing its carrier. The poller thread makes it runnable again when the socket is ready, and the read is tried again.

flashcards.front: Readiness model or completion model: which is epoll, and which is io_uring?
flashcards.back: epoll is readiness: the kernel says when you can do the I/O without waiting. io_uring is completion: you hand over the I/O, and the kernel says when it's done.

flashcards.front: Three places where io_uring gets switched off
flashcards.back: Docker's default seccomp filter (since Docker 25), Google's production servers and ChromeOS, and the kernel setting `kernel.io_uring_disabled` set to 1 or 2.

terms.plain: The kernel's store of bytes that have arrived on a socket and haven't been read yet.
A read that puts the thread to sleep until data is in the receive queue.
A socket flag that makes reads return at once. EAGAIN is the error that means "nothing yet, try again".
Linux's way to wait on many descriptors: register them once, then sleep until some are ready and get back only those.
epoll reports a descriptor for as long as it has data to read.
epoll reports a descriptor once each time new data arrives, so the program must read all of it.
One thread that waits for ready connections, handles each, and waits again. Java NIO and Netty are built on one.
A newer Linux way to do I/O: the program and the kernel share a submission queue and a completion queue, and the kernel does the work and reports when it's done.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate moved the payments program from one platform thread per connection to virtual threads. It now runs with about 30 operating-system threads instead of 2,000, although the code still calls a blocking `read()`. They ask you why. Explain what happens underneath, and what it doesn't change.
explain_back.answer: With platform threads, each connection had a real thread asleep in the kernel's `read()` until data arrived in that socket's receive queue. That's 2,000 kernel tasks, each with its own stack, almost all asleep. On virtual threads, the JDK makes every socket non-blocking. When our code reads and the queue is empty, the read fails with `EAGAIN` underneath. The JDK registers the socket with epoll, parks the virtual thread, and its carrier goes off to run another one. One poller thread sleeps in `epoll_wait` for all the sockets. When one has data, the JDK makes its virtual thread runnable again, and the read is tried again. So the kernel sees the carriers (one per CPU core), the poller and the JVM's own threads, about 30 in all, and `strace` shows reads failing with `EAGAIN`, each followed by `epoll_ctl`. What doesn't change: the CPU work per payment is the same, and a parked virtual thread still keeps its stack on the heap. Anything further along with its own limit, such as a database that takes only 20 connections at a time, still sets the pace. And waiting that the JDK can't turn into a park, such as a call into native code (code written in C rather than Java), still holds a carrier.

deeper.body:
Edge-triggered mode has a sibling, `EPOLLONESHOT`: report the socket once, then switch it off until the program turns it back on with `epoll_ctl(MOD)`. Groups of threads that share one epoll instance use it, so two threads never handle the same socket at once. `EPOLLEXCLUSIVE` attacks the opposite problem, the thundering herd: many threads waiting on one listening socket, all woken for a single new connection. And `SO_REUSEPORT` lets several sockets, one per thread, listen on the same port, with the kernel spreading new connections across them. That's how many servers spread `accept` across CPU cores.

Writing is the other half of a real event loop. `write()` on a non-blocking socket can write fewer bytes than you asked for, or fail with `EAGAIN`, when the socket's send queue is full because the client reads slowly. A server then keeps the rest, asks to be told when the socket can take more (`OP_WRITE`, `EPOLLOUT`), and writes again when the kernel says there's room. The lab's echo server skips that, because its messages are tiny. Netty's outbound buffer, with its high and low water marks, is the grown-up version.

io_uring keeps growing past files and sockets. It has operations for `accept`, `connect`, `openat`, `fsync` and more, chains of requests that run in order, buffers and files registered once to skip lookups on every call, and an `SQPOLL` mode where a kernel thread watches the submission queue, so the program makes no system calls at all while it's busy. That reach is also the security worry: each operation is kernel code running for the process, outside the paths that seccomp and other filters were built around.

Finally, `strace -c` measures time inside system calls, including time asleep. That's why the platform-thread server's `read` looked like the most expensive call in the Try it: it's where its threads wait. To find time spent waiting for the CPU instead, use `/proc/<pid>/schedstat` from CPU scheduling: EEVDF, nice and CPU quotas.
